overview.h1: HTS Chapter 01: Live Animals — Tariff Rates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 01: Live Animals — Tariff Rates & Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Complete searchable duty table for all 78 HTS Chapter 01 tariff lines — live horses, cattle, swine, sheep, goats, poultry and other live animals. General, FTA and Column 2 rates, filterable by product name.

overview.intro:
Chapter 01 covers animals imported alive — horses, cattle, swine, sheep and goats, poultry, and everything from honeybees to parrots. Its **78 tariff lines** carry some of the smallest printed rates in the schedule: a penny per kilogram on cattle, 68¢ per head on goats, 0.9¢ on a day-old chick.

The printed rate is rarely what decides the cost. Canada and Mexico supplied 79% of the $3.71B the U.S. imported in 2025, and USMCA-qualifying animals from both enter free. Animals from elsewhere pay the base rate **plus an extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies — 10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most others, +20% for China and +37.5% for Brazil (see Rates by country). And for any shipment, disease status, quarantine and permits decide whether it lands at all.

productGroups.label: Horses, asses, mules & hinnies
productGroups.blurb: Horses enter free whether or not they are purebred breeding animals. The duty sits on the other equines: asses at 6.8% and the residual mule/hinny line at 4.5%.

productGroups.label: Cattle & buffalo
productGroups.blurb: Purebred breeding cattle are free. Everything else — the feeder and slaughter cattle that make up almost all of the volume — carries 1¢/kg, which USMCA zeroes out for Canada and Mexico.

productGroups.label: Swine
productGroups.blurb: The only heading in the chapter with no duty anywhere: every swine line is free under the general rate.

productGroups.label: Sheep & goats
productGroups.blurb: Sheep are free; goats are 68¢ per head. Two lines, and the split between them is the whole story.

productGroups.label: Poultry
productGroups.blurb: Every poultry line is dutiable. Day-old chicks and poults (not over 185 g) are 0.9¢ each; mature birds are 2¢/kg.

productGroups.label: Other live animals
productGroups.blurb: The catch-all: mammals, reptiles, birds, insects. Most are free, but foxes are 4.8% and all live birds — birds of prey, parrots and other psittacines, ostriches and emus — are 1.8%.

workedExamples.title: 60 feeder steers from Alberta
workedExamples.body: The general rate is 1¢/kg, but Canada claims USMCA (SPI **S**), which is Free. At an average 350 kg a head the MFN duty would have been 60 × 350 kg × $0.01 = **$210**; under USMCA it is **$0**.

workedExamples.title: 500 goats from New Zealand
workedExamples.body: Goats are a flat 68¢ per head: 500 × $0.68 = **$340** base duty. New Zealand is one of the 60 economies in the 2026 Section 301 action, so another 12.5% of the shipment's value is added (9903.05.57). At $200 a head that is **$12,500**, so the extra duty, not the base rate, is most of the bill.

workedExamples.title: 50,000 day-old chicks
workedExamples.body: Chicks not over 185 g are 0.9¢ each: 50,000 × $0.009 = **$450** base duty. An FTA or AGOA claim removes the base rate (GSP, also listed on the line, has been expired since December 31, 2020), but a Section 301 duty for the country still applies — except under USMCA, where both are zero. Chicks from an HPAI-affected region cannot be imported at all (9 CFR 93.201).

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 01: Live Animals — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 01 Live Animals Tariff Updates — What Changed Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 01 (live animals) since January 2025: base rates on all 78 lines, the end of the IEEPA duties on Canada, Mexico and other countries, and the 2026 Section 301 tariffs, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). On every one of the 78 Chapter 01 lines the base rates are the same in both.

Everything that changed came on top of the base rate, as extra duties set by country. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada +35%, Mexico +25%, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, live animals from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%**; no Chapter 01 line is on the general exemption list. Two origins pay more because another duty stacks on top: China also pays the 7.5% List 4A duty (**20%** in all) and Brazil the separate 25% Brazil Section 301 duty (**37.5%** in all). **USMCA-qualifying animals from Canada and Mexico are still exempt.**
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 01 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the older China Section 301 List 4A, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: USMCA-qualifying goods entered free under USMCA: no Section 301 duty (9903.05.93), including lines whose general rate is already Free. The 2025 IEEPA duty on Canada (+35%, 9903.01.10) ended February 24, 2026. The 2026 Section 338 duties and import bans on Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy and motor vehicles (9903.03.12–9903.03.14) list no Chapter 01 line.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A USMCA-qualifying feeder steer from Alberta still pays $0; a Canadian animal that does not qualify pays the base rate plus 10% of value.

inEffect.exemption: USMCA-qualifying goods entered free under USMCA: no Section 301 duty (9903.05.94). The 2025 IEEPA duty on Mexico (+25%, 9903.01.01) ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: USMCA-qualifying cattle from Mexico pay nothing extra; animals that do not qualify pay the base rate plus 10% of value. Whether Mexican cattle can enter at all is decided by USDA APHIS (only Douglas, AZ is open as of October 7, 2026).

inEffect.exemption: For EU goods whose base rate (or its ad valorem equivalent) is under 10%, the total is 10% (9903.05.39); every Chapter 01 base rate is under 10%. The EU exception list (9903.05.97) has no Chapter 01 line. This replaced the 15% IEEPA reciprocal rate (9903.02.20), which ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A $50,000 horse from Germany, Ireland or the Netherlands pays $5,000 (10%).

inEffect.exemption: The UK exception list (9903.05.96) covers medical goods only, no Chapter 01 line.
inEffect.whatItMeans: A horse from the UK (Free base rate) pays 10% of its value.

inEffect.exemption: Two Section 301 duties stack: +12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31, from July 24, 2026) and +7.5% under List 4A (9903.88.15), which covers all 37 Chapter 01 subheadings and has been in force since 2019 (7.5% since February 14, 2020). The IEEPA duty on China ended February 24, 2026.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Live animals from China pay the base rate plus 20% of value; a 1.8% bird line pays 21.8%.

inEffect.measure: Section 301 tariffs: Brazil action plus 2026 forced-labor action
inEffect.exemption: +25% under the Brazil action from July 22, 2026 (9903.05.01) and +12.5% under the forced-labor action from July 24, 2026 (9903.05.27). Neither exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)–(v), U.S. note 52(b)–(e)) includes a Chapter 01 line.
inEffect.whatItMeans: Live animals from Brazil pay the base rate plus 37.5% of value.

inEffect.country: Other Section 301 economies (incl. Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan, Australia, New Zealand, India, Vietnam)
inEffect.exemption: Japan, South Korea and Switzerland pay 12.5% in total and Taiwan 10% in total when the base rate is lower (9903.05.49, 9903.05.71, 9903.05.74, 9903.05.76); Australia, New Zealand and Vietnam +12.5%; India +10%. Country exception lists in U.S. note 52(j) exempt a few 0106 lines (for example 0106.19.91 and 0106.20) for Switzerland, Taiwan, Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, Ecuador, Jordan, Argentina, Guatemala and El Salvador. Countries outside the 60 economies (for example Mauritius) pay no extra duty.
inEffect.whatItMeans: 500 goats from Australia: the 68¢/head base rate is Free under the Australia FTA, but the 12.5% Section 301 duty still applies to the shipment value.

changes.title: No Chapter 01 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 78 Chapter 01 tariff lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. Revision 21 changed only Chapter 38 and a China exclusion note in Chapter 99.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties and import bans do not reach live animals
changes.detail: Proclamations of September 8, 2026 moved some Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motor vehicles from the 50% Section 338 duty to an import ban from September 29, 2026, and changed the duty lists. The dairy ban list covers whey, molasses and non-alcoholic beer; the other two cover alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles. No Chapter 01 line is on the remaining duty lists (U.S. note 51, 9903.03.12–9903.03.14).

changes.title: Proposed: shorter HPAI waiting period for live birds and hatching eggs
changes.detail: APHIS proposed cutting the period in which live birds and other avian commodities may not have been exposed to HPAI, or sourced from HPAI-quarantined premises, before export to the United States from 90 days to 28 days. Comments are due November 23, 2026; the 90-day rule still applies.

changes.title: APHIS HPAI restrictions on Canadian poultry zones
changes.detail: Poultry, commercial birds, ratites and hatching eggs from or through a Canadian zone listed as Active or To be determined on the CFIA avian influenza list may not be imported. Pet and zoo birds from such zones must fly to JFK or Miami for a 30-day federal quarantine with testing; they may not enter by land.

changes.title: Douglas, AZ reopens to cattle from Mexico
changes.detail: USDA reopened the Douglas, Arizona port to Mexican cattle under a joint U.S.–Mexico screwworm protocol, with full inspection of every animal. Santa Teresa and Columbus, NM stay closed pending Mexico's progress on the Joint Action Plan (APHIS status page, updated October 7, 2026).

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties take effect; live animals not covered
changes.detail: 50% duties on certain Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy and motor vehicles (9903.03.12–9903.03.14) took effect after a 3-day suspension lapsed. No Chapter 01 line is on the lists in U.S. note 51.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover live animals
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). No Chapter 01 line is on the general exemption lists in U.S. note 52(b)–(e). EU goods pay 10% in total; Japan, South Korea and Switzerland 12.5% in total. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), with exemptions that include no Chapter 01 line. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 01 line was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03); USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75) renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025, when it had lapsed. AGOA (SPI D) makes every dutiable Chapter 01 line Free for listed sub-Saharan countries such as Mauritius, which is on the General Note 16 list in Revision 21. GSP (SPI A, A+) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Agricultural exemption did not cover live animals
changes.detail: The exemption lists in U.S. note 2(v)(iii)(a) (1,090 subheadings) and (v)(iii)(b) (17 articles) of Chapter 99 contained no Chapter 01 line, so the reciprocal duties applied to live animals until they ended on February 24, 2026.
changes.countries: All countries subject to the reciprocal tariff

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Southern border ports closed to Mexican cattle, bison and horses
changes.detail: USDA APHIS suspended imports of live cattle, bison and horses from Mexico through land-border ports after New World screwworm was detected further north in Veracruz. Horses may still enter by air under a screwworm protocol with quarantine.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of live animals fell from **$4.80B in 2024 to $3.71B in 2025** (-22.9%). Almost all of that is one lane: **cattle from Mexico** (heading 0102) went from $1.31B to $0.32B, a drop of $0.98B against a total drop of $1.10B. Canada grew over the same year.

The tariff schedule doesn't explain the Mexican drop. USMCA-qualifying cattle from Mexico paid no extra duty, and the base rate is unchanged. Animal health does: USDA APHIS closed the southern border ports to live cattle, bison and horses from Mexico on July 9, 2025 because of New World screwworm. The first port, Douglas, Arizona, reopened to cattle on August 24, 2026; Santa Teresa and Columbus, New Mexico were still closed on October 7, 2026.

The duty actually paid stays near zero because Canada and Mexico — 79% of 2025 imports — mostly enter under USMCA, and much of the rest of the chapter is duty-free under the general rate. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

Preferences: USMCA is applied for Canada and Mexico, and AGOA (SPI D) for Mauritius. AGOA was reauthorized on February 3, 2026 through December 31, 2026, retroactive to September 30, 2025 (P.L. 119-75; USTR). GSP (SPI A, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020 and Congress had not renewed it as of October 9, 2026 (CBP; HTS General Note 4 in Revision 21), so GSP claims pay the general rate. Other FTA preferences are not applied; they remove the base rate but not the Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)).

"Any other country" shows the range from no extra duty (countries outside the 60 Section 301 economies) to Brazil's +37.5%. Country exception lists in U.S. note 52(j) exempt a few 0106 lines for some countries; they are not applied in the matrix.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.
The rate is not the only gate: live cattle, bison and horses from Mexico can cross only at ports USDA APHIS has opened (Douglas, AZ as of October 7, 2026).

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 01: Live Animals — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Live Animals: Required Documents, Permits & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 01) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The permits, certificates and rules for each HTS Chapter 01 line — USDA APHIS, Fish & Wildlife, CDC — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, purebred breeding entries, Chapter 98 provisions.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For live animals the tariff is rarely the hard part — **the paperwork decides whether the animals land at all**. Every line in this chapter needs USDA animal-health clearance, and wildlife, birds and dogs add Fish & Wildlife and CDC rules.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule itself: claim **USMCA**, use the **purebred breeding** lines, or a **Chapter 98** provision when the purpose fits. Each one depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on animals from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The Section 301 duty — 10% of value for Canada or Mexico — plus any base rate
levers.appliesTo: All 78 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a prescribed format; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Claiming without a valid certification exposes the entry to the 10% Section 301 duty plus penalties. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Enter registered breeding stock under the "purebred breeding animals" lines
levers.saves: Cattle: Free instead of 1¢/kg · Buffalo: Free instead of 1¢/kg — about $5 on a 500 kg animal at 1¢/kg. The Section 301 duty for the country still applies.
levers.document: The schedule defines purebred breeding animals as animals certified by USDA as purebred of a recognized breed and registered in a recognized book of record. But the schedule itself notes that the USDA certificate of pure breeding is obsolete and can no longer be obtained — ask CBP what evidence it will accept before importing.
levers.caveat: 19 CFR 10.70 still describes the old certificate process; follow CBP's current guidance, not the regulation text.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision when the purpose fits
levers.saves: The base rate: each provision below is Free in the schedule
levers.appliesTo: Animals imported for a specific purpose, whatever their Chapter 01 line
levers.document: Evidence of the qualifying purpose (and, for 9813.00.60, a bond for temporary importation).
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duties (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) do not apply to goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision when CBP agrees the entry is appropriate, except entries under 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 (U.S. note 52(a) to Chapter 99 subchapter III); the Brazil duty (9903.05.01) has the same rule (U.S. note 50(a)). The entry must qualify, so get CBP's agreement (or a ruling) before relying on it.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about importing live animals into the U.S. — tariffs by country, HS codes and entry requirements. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: USMCA-qualifying animals from Canada and Mexico enter free — no base rate, no extra duty.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the extra duty is a Section 301 tariff: 10% in total for the EU, +10% or +12.5% for most other large suppliers, +20% for China and +37.5% for Brazil.
For live animals, USDA animal-health rules decide whether a shipment lands at all — Mexican cattle can cross only at Douglas, AZ as of October 2026. Check APHIS before every import.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on cattle from Canada?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on canadian cattle
faqs.answer: Not if they qualify for USMCA. Most cattle enter under 0102.29, with a base rate of 1¢/kg that USMCA makes Free, and USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the 10% Section 301 duty on Canadian products (9903.05.93). Cattle that don't qualify pay 1¢/kg plus 10% of their value (9903.05.29). The 35% IEEPA duty of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026. Canada shipped $1.82B of cattle to the U.S. in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on horses from Canada?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on horses from canada
faqs.answer: Horses have a Free base rate. With a USMCA claim they stay free; horses that don't qualify for USMCA pay 10% of their value under the Section 301 duty on Canadian products (9903.05.29). The 35% IEEPA duty ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on horses from Europe — Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands?
searchedAs: import duty on horses from ireland
tariffs on horses imported from europe
faqs.answer: 10% of the horse's value since July 24, 2026. For EU products whose base rate is under 10%, the Section 301 action charges 10% in place of the base rate (9903.05.39), and horses are Free at base. The 15% reciprocal rate of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026. Horses brought in temporarily for breeding, shows or competition can enter under 9813.00.60 (Free, under bond); the Section 301 duty does not apply to goods properly entered under a Chapter 98 provision when CBP agrees the entry is appropriate (U.S. note 52(a); only 9802 entries are excepted). The U.S. imported $380M of horses and other equines from these five EU countries in 2025.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to import a horse from Europe to the U.S.?
searchedAs: how much does it cost to import a horse from europe to us
how much does it cost to import a horse from germany
cost to import horse from europe to usa
faqs.answer: The tariff part is 10% of the horse's value — $5,000 on a $50,000 horse (EU, 9903.05.39). On top of that come USDA requirements: an import permit, arrival at a designated port, inspection and quarantine (9 CFR 93.304, 93.306, 93.308). Transport and quarantine fees are not covered here.

faqs.question: Why did cattle imports from Mexico stop?
searchedAs: why do we import cattle from mexico
faqs.answer: Imports of Mexican cattle fell from $1.31B in 2024 to $324M in 2025. Tariffs don't explain it: USMCA-qualifying cattle from Mexico pay no extra duty and the base rate didn't change. Animal health does — USDA APHIS closed the southern border ports to cattle, bison and horses from Mexico on July 9, 2025 because of New World screwworm. Douglas, Arizona reopened to cattle on August 24, 2026; Santa Teresa and Columbus, New Mexico were still closed as of October 7, 2026. Check APHIS for the current status.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for live cattle?
faqs.answer: Heading 0102 (live bovine animals). Purebred breeding cattle are 0102.21 (Free); other cattle are 0102.29 (1¢/kg) — the most traded product in the chapter, $2.08B in 2025. Buffalo are 0102.31 and 0102.39. The 10-digit U.S. lines split further by use, weight and sex.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for live animals?
faqs.answer: Chapter 01: headings 0101 (horses, asses, mules), 0102 (cattle, buffalo), 0103 (swine), 0104 (sheep, goats), 0105 (poultry) and 0106 (all other live animals), split into 78 ten-digit U.S. lines. Live fish and other aquatic animals are in Chapter 03, not here.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for live chickens?
faqs.answer: 0105.11 for chicks weighing not more than 185 g (0.9¢ each), and 0105.94 for larger chickens (2¢/kg). Live poultry and hatching eggs cannot come from or through a region with highly pathogenic avian influenza or Newcastle disease, or from H5/H7-vaccinated flocks (9 CFR 93.201), and need an APHIS permit and a 30-day quarantine unless they come from an unrestricted part of Canada.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a dog, and what do I need to bring one into the U.S.?
searchedAs: bringing a dog into the us from canada
importing a dog into the us
faqs.answer: Dogs are 0106.19.91.20, with a Free base rate. Entry is governed by CDC rules — including the CDC dog import form and a microchip (42 CFR 71.51). Commercial imports from one of the 60 Section 301 economies can owe +10% or +12.5%; see the rates by country.

faqs.question: Can I import a parrot into the U.S.?
faqs.answer: Only within tight limits. Parrots are 0106.32 (1.8% base rate, plus any Section 301 duty for the country of origin), but the Wild Bird Conservation Act restricts imports of exotic birds (50 CFR part 15), most parrots need CITES permits (50 CFR part 23), and USDA requires an import permit, health certificate and quarantine (9 CFR 93.103, 93.104, 93.106), plus Fish & Wildlife Form 3-177. Birds from a region with highly pathogenic avian influenza face extra limits (9 CFR 93.101).

faqs.question: How many live animals does the U.S. import?
faqs.answer: $3.71B of live animals in 2025, of which $2.14B was live cattle and other bovine animals (heading 0102). Canada supplied 70% of the total; Mexico, still the No. 2 source, fell from $1.31B to $329M as its cattle shipments dropped.
